title: The number seven
summary: From the creation week to the seven seals, trumpets and bowls, seven marks what God completes.

stops.note: God finishes his work and rests on the seventh day, blessing it and making it holy.
The covenant curses warn that persistent rebellion will bring discipline 'sevenfold', a pattern repeated four times in the chapter.
Seven priests carry seven trumpets around Jericho for seven days, and seven times on the seventh day, before the walls fall.
The Spirit rests on the coming branch of Jesse; the Greek and Latin versions list seven gifts here, a list later read as the sevenfold Spirit.
A lampstand with seven lamps, explained as the seven eyes of the LORD ranging through the earth, stands beside the word 'not by might, but by my Spirit'.
Jesus turns Peter's generous 'seven times' into seventy times seven (or seventy-seven), forgiveness without limit.
Grace comes from the one who is, was and is to come, and from 'the seven spirits who are before his throne'.
The slain Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes, 'which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth', joining Zechariah's lamp-eyes to the Lamb.
The seven last plagues are called last 'for with them the wrath of God is finished', seven as completion.

meaning: Seven is the Bible's number of completeness and of God's finished work, rooted in the creation week and the Sabbath. It structures worship (the seventh day, seventh year and jubilee), judgment (the sevenfold curses) and victory (Jericho). In Revelation it marks fullness: seven churches stand for the whole church, the seven spirits for the fullness of God's Spirit, and the series of seven judgments for God's purposes brought to completion.
culture: Seven-day sequences and sevenfold patterns were common across the Ancient Near East, from the seven days of the flood in the Gilgamesh epic to seven-day cycles in Ugaritic poetry. At Qumran the community kept a 364-day calendar built on weeks, and the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice arrange angelic praise in sevens. In the Greco-Roman world the seven planets and the seven stars of the Pleiades or the Bear were familiar, and imperial coins sometimes showed a ruler holding stars, a background some commentators hear behind the seven stars in Christ's hand.
compare: Revelation uses seven more systematically than any other biblical book: seven churches, spirits, lampstands, stars, seals, trumpets, thunders and bowls, plus sevenfold lists of praise and of 'blessed' sayings. It combines Zechariah's seven lamps and eyes with the Lamb, so that the Spirit's fullness belongs to the crucified Christ. The Jericho pattern of seven trumpets reappears on a cosmic scale, now against the whole world-system rather than one city.
views: Historicists have often read the seven churches and the seven seals and trumpets as successive periods of church history, while futurists usually read the judgment series as future events and preterists as judgments of the first century. Idealists, and many interpreters of every school, stress that the sevens are a literary structure signalling completeness rather than a timetable.

title: Twelve and the 144,000
summary: The twelve tribes and twelve apostles become the sealed 144,000 and the city of twelve gates and twelve foundations.

stops.note: Jacob's blessings close with 'all these are the twelve tribes of Israel', the founding number of God's people.
The high priest carries twelve stones engraved with the names of the tribes on his breastpiece before the LORD.
Moses counts by tribe every man twenty years and older able to go to war, a military census of Israel in the wilderness.
Elijah rebuilds the altar on Carmel with twelve stones for the twelve tribes, though the kingdom is divided.
The restored city has twelve gates named for the tribes, and its name is 'The LORD is there'.
Jesus promises the twelve that they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
John hears the number of the sealed, 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve listed tribes.
The 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion with his name and his Father's name on their foreheads.
The new Jerusalem has twelve gates with the tribes' names, twelve foundations with the apostles' names, and measures 12,000 stadia with a wall of 144 cubits.

meaning: Twelve is the number of the people of God, first as the tribes of Israel and then as the apostles whom Jesus chose to reconstitute that people around himself. Twelve times twelve times a thousand (144,000) multiplies this number into a vast and complete people. In the new Jerusalem tribes and apostles together form the city's gates and foundations, one people built on both.
culture: Hopes for the regathering of all twelve tribes were alive in Second Temple Judaism, long after the northern tribes had been scattered. The Qumran War Scroll organises the end-time army of the sons of light by tribes, and the Community Rule speaks of a council of twelve men. Military musters by tribe, as in Numbers 1, form the background that Richard Bauckham sees behind Revelation 7, where the sealed are counted like an army.
compare: Revelation 7 echoes the census of Numbers 1, but John hears 144,000 and then sees an innumerable multitude from every nation, a pairing many read as two views of the same people, while others keep them distinct. The tribal list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and Joseph and Manasseh replace Ephraim. Revelation 21 then joins Israel's twelve and the apostles' twelve in one city whose measurements are multiples of twelve.
views: Many futurists, especially dispensationalists, take the 144,000 as Jewish believers sealed during a future tribulation, while preterists often see Jewish Christians of the first century protected in the war with Rome. Historicists and idealists commonly read the number symbolically as the whole people of God, sealed and counted as an army, and identical with the great multitude.

title: Three and a half, 1,260 days, 42 months
summary: Daniel's 'time, times and half a time' becomes Revelation's limited season of trouble and witness.

stops.note: After 'many days', in the third year of drought, the word of the LORD sends Elijah back to Ahab.
The little horn speaks against the Most High and wears out the saints 'for a time, times, and half a time'.
In the middle of the seventieth week sacrifice and offering cease, splitting the seven into two halves.
The man in linen swears that the end of these wonders will be after 'a time, times, and half a time', followed by 1,290 and 1,335 days.
Jesus says the heavens were shut in Elijah's day 'three years and six months'.
James repeats that Elijah prayed and it did not rain for three years and six months.
The holy city is trampled for forty-two months while the two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days, with power to shut the sky like Elijah.
The woman is nourished in the wilderness for 1,260 days, also called 'a time, and times, and half a time' in 12:14.
The beast is given authority to act for forty-two months.

meaning: Three and a half is half of seven: a broken, interrupted and limited span. It names a season when evil seems to prevail and God's people suffer, yet the time is measured and cut short by God. Revelation gives the same period three ways (42 months, 1,260 days, time, times and half a time) and assigns it both to the oppressor's rule and to the church's protected witness.
culture: The persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, when the temple altar was defiled from late 167 until its rededication in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52-54), gave Daniel's readers a concrete experience of a little over three years of desolation. Jewish tradition had already stretched Elijah's drought, set 'in the third year' in 1 Kings, to three and a half years, as both Luke and James show. Readers in Roman Asia could also recall that the Roman campaign against Judea, from spring 67 to the fall of Jerusalem in August 70, lasted roughly three and a half years.
compare: Revelation takes Daniel's period of the little horn and splits its meaning: the same span is the beast's season and the witnesses' season of Elijah-like prophecy and protection. The Elijah echo turns the period into a time of testimony, not only of suffering. Unlike Daniel 12, Revelation does not add the extra 1,290 and 1,335 days.
views: Preterists often connect the period with the Jewish War of AD 67 to 70 or with Nero's persecution, and futurists with the second half of a future seven-year tribulation. Historicists apply the day-for-a-year principle (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6) to get 1,260 years, often dated 538 to 1798 for papal power. Idealists read it as the whole church age between Christ's first and second comings.

title: A thousand years
summary: A number of fullness and of God's long patience becomes the reign of the saints in Revelation 20.

stops.note: Adam lives 930 years; later Jewish tradition noted he died short of a thousand, a 'day' in God's sight.
God keeps covenant and steadfast love 'to a thousand generations' with those who love him.
God owns 'the cattle on a thousand hills', a thousand as a round number for all.
A thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday when it is past, or a watch in the night.
In the new heavens and new earth one who dies at a hundred will be thought a youth, a text often linked with a coming age of long life.
With the Lord one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day, so the delay of his coming is patience.
An angel binds Satan for a thousand years so that he may not deceive the nations any longer.
Those who were faithful come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years in the first resurrection.

meaning: In the Old Testament a thousand is usually a large round number expressing abundance or completeness, as in 'a thousand generations' or 'a thousand hills'. Psalm 90 and 2 Peter use it to contrast God's time with human time. Revelation 20 applies it to the binding of Satan and the reign of the faithful with Christ, the only place the Bible links a thousand years to such a reign.
culture: Several Jewish writings spoke of a temporary messianic age before the final judgment, though with different lengths: 4 Ezra 7:28-29 gives four hundred years, and 2 Baruch 29 to 30 a limited period of plenty. Jubilees 4:30 explains that Adam died seventy years short of a thousand because a thousand years is one day in heaven, and 2 Enoch 33 (of disputed date) speaks of a world-week of seven thousand years followed by an eighth. The Epistle of Barnabas 15 shows early Christians also reading the creation week as six thousand years followed by a sabbath rest.
compare: Revelation draws on the Jewish hope of an interim kingdom but gives it a distinct shape: the reign belongs to Christ and to martyrs and faithful witnesses, not to an earthly national restoration described in detail. Where Psalm 90 and 2 Peter use a thousand years to relativise human time, Revelation uses it for a defined era of victory between Satan's binding and his final release. The new heavens and earth of Isaiah 65 are placed after this period in Revelation 21.
views: Premillennialists, both historic and dispensational, expect a future reign of Christ on earth after his return, and dispensationalists usually take the thousand years literally. Amillennialists read it symbolically as the present reign of Christ and the saints between his two comings, and postmillennialists as a long era of gospel triumph before his return; preterist and idealist readers usually hold one of these last two views.

title: 666, the number of a man
summary: A riddle for the wise: a name counted in letters, Solomon's gold, and six that never reaches seven.

stops.note: Israel's king must not greatly multiply silver and gold for himself, nor wives who turn his heart away.
The gold that came to Solomon in one year weighed 666 talents, at the height of his wealth and just before his turn to idols.
The Chronicler repeats the figure of 666 talents of gold for Solomon's yearly income.
Among the returning exiles were the sons of Adonikam, 666, the only other place this figure appears in the Old Testament (Nehemiah 7:18 gives 667).
Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image sixty cubits high and six wide and orders all peoples to worship it on pain of death.
Paul describes the man of lawlessness who exalts himself and takes his seat in the temple of God, a figure often read beside the beast.
No one may buy or sell without the mark, the name of the beast or the number of its name; 'it is the number of a man, and his number is 666'.
The victors stand beside the sea of glass, having conquered the beast, its image and the number of its name.

meaning: Revelation presents 666 as a riddle calling for wisdom and calculation, most naturally the numerical value of a name. Biblically the figure carries echoes of royal greed and idolatry (Solomon's gold, Nebuchadnezzar's image of sixes) and of human power claiming divine honour. Many also see a contrast with seven: a triple six that falls short of completeness, set against the Lamb and his followers.
culture: Ancient Hebrew and Greek used letters as numerals, so every name had a numerical value; the practice is called gematria (Greek isopsephia). A graffito at Pompeii reads 'I love her whose number is 545', and the Sibylline Oracles (1:324-330) give the value of the Greek name Jesus as 888. Written in Hebrew letters, the Greek form 'Neron Caesar' totals 666, while the Latin form 'Nero Caesar' totals 616, the reading found in some manuscripts (including Papyrus 115) and known to Irenaeus; a Murabba'at papyrus shows the spelling 'qsr' for Caesar in use. Bauckham notes that 666 is a doubly triangular number and that 'beast' (therion) transliterated into Hebrew letters also gives 666.
compare: Revelation turns the Old Testament's quiet number of royal wealth into a public test of allegiance tied to buying and selling. Daniel's image that all must worship returns as the image of the beast, with economic exclusion added to the threat of death. Against the beast's number stands the Lamb's name on the foreheads of the 144,000 (14:1).
views: Preterists usually identify the number with Nero Caesar, supported by the 616 variant, while historicists have proposed names such as Lateinos (already suggested by Irenaeus) or papal titles. Futurists generally expect it to fit the name of a future Antichrist and caution against premature identifications. Idealists stress the symbolism of six falling short of seven, though many interpreters combine a first-century reference with a lasting symbolic meaning.

title: The seal and the mark on forehead and hand
summary: God's people bear his name on forehead and hand; the beast's followers bear a counterfeit mark.

stops.note: The feast of unleavened bread is to be 'a sign on your hand and a memorial between your eyes', so the LORD's law is in your mouth.
A gold plate engraved 'Holy to the LORD' is fastened on Aaron's turban, on his forehead, as he bears Israel's guilt before God.
The commands of the Shema are to be bound as a sign on the hand and as frontlets between the eyes.
In the coming outpouring of the Spirit, one will write on his hand 'The LORD's', a sign of belonging.
A man with a writing case puts a mark (the Hebrew letter taw) on the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's abominations, and they are spared.
Believers are sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the guarantee of their inheritance.
An angel holding the seal of the living God orders the winds held back until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads.
The second beast causes all to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell.
In the new Jerusalem God's servants will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.

meaning: A mark or seal shows ownership, protection and allegiance. In the Law, God's word on hand and forehead means that action and thought belong to him, and the high priest's forehead plate declares Israel holy to the LORD. In Ezekiel and Revelation the mark separates those spared from judgment, and in the New Testament the seal is the Holy Spirit; the beast's mark is a rival claim on the same hand and forehead.
culture: Devout Jews wore tefillin (phylacteries) on arm and forehead, and examples have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Psalms of Solomon (15:6-9) describe a mark of God on the righteous for salvation and a mark of destruction on sinners' foreheads, and 3 Maccabees 2:29 tells of Jews forced to be branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus. In the Roman world slaves, runaways and sometimes soldiers could be branded or tattooed, seals (sphragis) marked documents and goods as owned, and the Greek word for 'mark' (charagma) was used for imperial stamps on documents and the impress on coins. Membership in the trade guilds of Asian cities, with their patron gods and feasts, could also shape who prospered in buying and selling.
compare: Revelation combines Ezekiel's protective forehead mark with the priestly 'Holy to the LORD' and the Shema's sign on hand and forehead. The beast's mark is a parody of God's seal, applied to the very places where Israel was told to bind God's word. The story ends not with a seal for protection but with God's own name on the foreheads of those who see his face.
views: Preterists often link the mark to participation in the imperial cult or to the economic pressure of Roman Asia, and some historicists, including Seventh-day Adventists, to allegiance to a false worship system set against the seal of God. Futurists usually expect a literal mark required for commerce under a future Antichrist, sometimes linked to technology. Idealists read forehead and hand as thought and action, so that the mark is visible allegiance shown in life.

title: The scroll and the book of life
summary: Sealed scrolls, eaten scrolls and the book of the living run from Sinai to the last judgment.

stops.note: Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book if Israel is not forgiven; God replies that he blots out those who have sinned against him.
The psalmist prays that his enemies be blotted out of the book of the living and not enrolled among the righteous.
The prophetic vision has become to the people like the words of a sealed book that no one can read.
Ezekiel is handed a scroll written on front and back with lament and woe, and when he eats it, it is sweet as honey.
Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end; in 12:1 all whose names are found written in the book are delivered.
A book of remembrance is written before the LORD for those who feared him and esteemed his name.
Paul speaks of his fellow workers 'whose names are in the book of life'.
A scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals, can be opened only by the Lion of Judah who is the slain Lamb.
The dead are judged from what is written in the books, and another book is opened, the book of life.

meaning: Scrolls carry God's purposes and words, sometimes hidden until the time appointed and sometimes given to prophets to absorb and proclaim. The book of life is the register of those who belong to God, from Moses' prayer to the last judgment. Revelation brings both together: the sealed scroll of God's plan is opened by the Lamb, and the book of life is 'the Lamb's book of life'.
culture: Ancient legal documents were often sealed, sometimes with an open copy kept alongside, as in Jeremiah's purchase deed (Jeremiah 32:10-14), and under Roman practice a will was sealed by seven witnesses and opened only when the testator died. Writing on both sides of a scroll (an opisthograph) was unusual and signals a full text. 1 Enoch and Jubilees speak of heavenly tablets recording deeds and destinies, and Greek cities kept registers of citizens from which the names of the condemned could be erased, background often cited for Revelation 3:5 at Sardis.
compare: Daniel is told to seal his book for the end, but John is told not to seal his (Revelation 22:10), because the time is near. Ezekiel's eaten scroll returns in Revelation 10, where the little scroll is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach, recommissioning John as a prophet. The book of life moves from a register of the living to a register owned by the slain Lamb, whose names cannot be erased for those who overcome (3:5).
views: Interpreters differ on the scroll's content: many see God's plan of judgment and redemption, others a covenant deed or testament, and some the Old Testament now opened in Christ. Futurists tend to read the opening of the seals as a future sequence, preterists as judgments of the first century, historicists as a sequence through church history, and idealists as patterns recurring throughout the age.

title: Trumpets
summary: The trumpet of Sinai, Jericho and the day of the LORD sounds again in Revelation's seven trumpets.

stops.note: A very loud trumpet blast, growing louder and louder, accompanies the LORD's descent on Sinai in thunder, lightning and smoke.
The first day of the seventh month is a solemn rest, 'a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets'.
When Israel goes to war it is to sound an alarm on the trumpets, and 'you shall be remembered before the LORD your God'.
Seven priests blow seven ram's-horn trumpets and the walls of Jericho fall at the long blast and the people's shout.
'Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm', for the day of the LORD is coming, a day of darkness.
The Son of Man sends his angels with a loud trumpet call to gather his elect from the four winds.
The Lord descends with a cry of command, the archangel's voice and the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ rise first.
The seven angels prepare to blow their trumpets, and the first brings hail and fire mixed with blood on the earth.
At the seventh trumpet loud voices announce that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.

meaning: Trumpets announce God's presence (Sinai), summon to worship and remembrance (the feasts), sound the alarm of war and judgment (Numbers, Joel) and herald victory (Jericho). In the New Testament the trumpet marks the Lord's coming, the gathering of his people and the resurrection. Revelation's trumpets are warnings of judgment that call to repentance and end in the proclamation of God's kingdom.
culture: Israel used both the ram's horn (shofar) and silver trumpets (Numbers 10:2), and the later Jewish daily prayer asks God to 'sound the great shofar for our freedom', echoing Isaiah 27:13. The Qumran War Scroll gives detailed instructions for trumpets inscribed with battle slogans in the final war. Roman armies in Asia and elsewhere used the tuba and other horns to signal attack and retreat, so a trumpet sequence would also sound military to John's hearers.
compare: Revelation fuses Jericho's seven trumpets with the Exodus plagues: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness and locusts return as trumpet judgments. Unlike the plagues on Egypt these strike a third of creation, warnings held in check, and the seventh trumpet turns from judgment to the announcement of the kingdom. The 'last trumpet' of Paul (1 Corinthians 15:52) and the trumpet of 1 Thessalonians 4:16 are linked to the seventh trumpet by some readers and kept distinct by others.
views: Preterists commonly link the trumpets to judgments on Judea and Jerusalem in the war with Rome, and classic historicists to the barbarian invasions of Rome, the rise of Islam and the Ottoman Turks. Futurists see future judgments in sequence after the seals, and idealists see recurring warnings through the church age, often parallel to the seals and bowls. Rapture views differ on whether the seventh trumpet is Paul's 'last trumpet'.

title: Horns and coloured horses
summary: Horns stand for power and kings; coloured horses patrol the earth from Zechariah to the four riders.

stops.note: Joseph's might is like the horns of a wild ox, with which he gores the peoples.
The fourth beast has ten horns, and a little horn with eyes and a boastful mouth uproots three of them.
A ram with two horns is trampled by a goat with a conspicuous horn, later explained as the kings of Media-Persia and Greece (8:20-21).
A man on a red horse, with red, sorrel and white horses behind him, reports that they have patrolled the earth and it is at rest.
Four chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses go out to the four winds of heaven.
Zechariah blesses God who has raised up 'a horn of salvation' in the house of David.
The Lamb who was slain has seven horns, fullness of power held by the crucified one.
As the Lamb opens the first four seals, riders go out on white, red, black and pale horses, bringing conquest, war, famine and death.
The ten horns of the beast are ten kings who receive authority for one hour with the beast.

meaning: A horn is a biblical image of strength and royal power, whether of a tribe, a king, an empire or God's anointed. Horses are instruments of war and of swift royal patrol, and their colours in Zechariah and Revelation suggest the character of their missions: red for bloodshed, black for famine, pale (Greek chloros, yellowish-green) for death, white for conquest or victory. Revelation sets the Lamb's seven horns against the beast's ten horns, true and false power.
culture: Mesopotamian gods and kings wore horned crowns as signs of divinity and might, as on the victory stele of Naram-Sin, and Hellenistic coins showed Alexander with the ram's horns of Zeus Ammon and Seleucus I in a horned helmet, close to Daniel 8's ram and goat. The Persian royal courier and patrol system lies behind Zechariah's horses reporting on the earth. In the first century the mounted archers of Parthia were Rome's feared eastern rivals, a likely echo in the bow-carrying rider on the white horse, and the price in Revelation 6:6 (a day's wage for a quart of wheat) reflects famine conditions known in the eastern empire.
compare: Revelation reworks Zechariah's patrolling horses, whose colours partly match, into agents of judgment released by the Lamb, and orders them into a sequence of conquest, war, famine and death. It merges Daniel's four beasts into one beast with ten horns, while giving the Lamb seven horns, so power is redefined by sacrifice. The white horse returns in 19:11 with Christ as its rider, prompting debate over whether the first rider is Christ or a counterfeit.
views: The first rider has been read as Christ or the gospel (by many historicists and some idealists), as a counterfeit Antichrist (many futurists) or as Roman or Parthian conquest (many preterists). The ten horns have been taken as client kings or rulers of the Roman world (preterist), the kingdoms that arose from Rome's breakup (historicist), a future ten-nation alliance (futurist), or the fullness of earthly powers aligned with evil (idealist).

title: White garments and robes washed in blood
summary: From scarlet sins made white as snow to robes washed white in the Lamb's blood.

stops.note: Judah 'washes his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes', a royal image later read messianically.
David prays, 'Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow'.
'Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow'.
The Ancient of Days takes his throne, his clothing white as snow and his hair like pure wool.
Some of the wise will stumble so that they may be refined, purified and made white until the time of the end.
Joshua the high priest's filthy garments are removed, his iniquity taken away, and he is clothed in pure vestments and a clean turban.
At the transfiguration Jesus' face shines like the sun and his clothes become white as light.
Those in white robes have come out of the great tribulation and 'washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb'.
The bride is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, 'the righteous deeds of the saints'.

meaning: White garments signify purity, cleansing from sin, heavenly glory and victory. Cleansing is God's gift (Isaiah 1, Zechariah 3) but also comes through testing and faithfulness (Daniel 11). In Revelation the white robes belong to God and his angels, to the elders and to the faithful who overcome, and they are made white by the Lamb's blood.
culture: Israel's priests served in white linen, especially on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4), and Josephus reports that the Essenes wore white (Jewish War 2.123, 2.137). 1 Enoch 62:15-16 promises the righteous 'garments of glory' that will not wear out. In the Roman world white togas were worn by candidates for office and on festival days, and white clothing marked celebrants of victory; Sardis, addressed in Revelation 3:4-5, was known for its wool and dyeing trade.
compare: Revelation intensifies Isaiah's paradox: scarlet sins made white becomes robes washed white in blood, cleansing through the death of the Lamb. Daniel's Ancient of Days in white (Daniel 7:9) becomes the risen Christ with white hair in Revelation 1:14, and the faithful share his whiteness. The image of washed garments also recalls Genesis 49:11, while the rider's robe dipped in blood (19:13) draws on Isaiah 63's garments stained in judgment.
views: The white-robed multitude of Revelation 7 is read by many futurists as those saved and often martyred in a future great tribulation, by preterists as believers who came through first-century persecution, by historicists as the redeemed through the tribulations of church history, and by idealists as the whole church triumphant. Readers differ on whether 'the righteous deeds of the saints' (19:8) stresses God's gift, faithful living, or both.
